entry: Belief that the divine intersects every part of the universe and also extends beyond space and time. The term was coined in 1828 by German philosopher Karl Christian Friedrich Krause, who sought to distinguish the ideas of [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel]] and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling from the supposed pantheism of [[Baruch Spinoza]]. Unlike [[Pantheism|pantheism]], which identifies God with the universe, panentheism holds that God is greater than the universe, which some versions describe as a manifestation of God. Much of [[Hinduism|Hindu]] thought is characterized by panentheism. Process thinkers [[Alfred North Whitehead]] and Charles Hartshorne developed panentheistic frameworks, and the idea influenced New England transcendentalists such as [[Ralph Waldo Emerson]]. Critics argue that it blurs the boundary between creator and creation, while supporters see it as reconciling unity and plurality.

Supercontinent that existed during the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic eras. It assembled from the continental units of [[Gondwana]], Euramerica and [[Siberia]] during the [[Carboniferous]] period, about 335 million years ago, and began to break apart about 175 million years ago, at the beginning of the [[Jurassic]]. It was C-shaped, with most of its mass stretching between Earth's northern and southern polar regions, and it was surrounded by the superocean Panthalassa. It is the most recent supercontinent to have existed and was the first to be reconstructed by geologists. [[Alfred Wegener]] proposed the concept in 1912 as part of his theory of continental drift. His proposed mechanism, [[Centrifugal force|centrifugal force]] from Earth's rotation, proved implausible, so Arthur Holmes's mantle convection and later seafloor mapping helped lead to [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. Evidence includes the matching coastlines of the Atlantic continents, glacial deposits of the same age on separate continents, and similar or identical fossil species now far apart.

Mammal of the order Pholidota, also called a scaly anteater. The one extant family, Manidae, has three genera. *Manis* has five species in Asia, while *Phataginus* and *Smutsia* have two species each in sub-Saharan Africa. Pangolins range from 30 to 100 cm (12 to 39 in) in size and are covered in large keratin scales that harden as the animal matures. They are nocturnal and feed mainly on [[Ant|ants]] and [[Termite|termites]], which they catch with long tongues. Most species are solitary, and when threatened they curl into a ball. Poaching for meat and scales, used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]], and deforestation threaten them, and they are among the most trafficked mammals in the world. As of January 2020, eight species were listed as threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Confederation of Eurasian nomads that established the Avar Khaganate in the Carpathian Basin. The name Pannonian Avars, after Pannonia in the upper Danube basin, distinguishes them from the Avars of the [[Caucasus]]. Known in Byzantine sources as Pseudo-Avars, they entered history in the mid-6th century on the Pontic–Caspian steppe, having fled the rule of the [[Göktürks]]. Their khaganate lasted from the late 6th to the early 9th century CE, and they exerted influence over Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe. They are best known for their wars with the [[Byzantine Empire]] from 568 to 626 and for their influence on the Slavic migrations to the [[Balkans]]. Archaeogenetic studies suggest that they originated in present-day [[Mongolia]] and may descend from remnants of the Rouran Khaganate. Campaigns by [[Charlemagne]] and the [[Franks]] dismantled Avar power by 803–811 CE.

Sexual, romantic, or emotional attraction to people regardless of their sex or gender identity. Pansexual people may describe themselves as gender-blind. Pansexuality is sometimes treated as a sexual orientation in its own right and sometimes as a branch of [[Bisexuality]]. The prefix comes from [[Ancient Greek]] *pan*, meaning *all*. The forms *pansexual* and *pansexualism* were first attested in 1914, coined by opponents of [[Sigmund Freud]] for the idea that the sex instinct drives all human activity. Pansexuality is sometimes called omnisexuality.

American heavy metal band formed in Arlington, [[Texas]], in 1981 by the Abbott brothers, guitarist Dimebag Darrell and drummer Vinnie Paul. The band popularized groove metal in the 1990s with *Cowboys from Hell* (1990) and *Vulgar Display of Power* (1992). *Far Beyond Driven* (1994) debuted at number one on the Billboard 200, and Pantera has sold around 20 million records worldwide. Internal conflict led to a breakup in 2003. On December 8, 2004, Dimebag Darrell was shot dead on stage in [[Columbus, Ohio]]. Phil Anselmo and Rex Brown began touring under the Pantera name in 2022.

Diverse family of philosophical and religious beliefs that equate reality with divinity. Pantheist beliefs hold that the totality of being, called Nature, the universe, or the cosmos, is a self-organizing unity that needs no distinct, supernatural creator. Pantheists do not recognize a personal god. One of the earliest uses of the term dates to a 1697 book by mathematician Joseph Raphson. The idea was popularized in Western culture by [[Baruch Spinoza]], especially in his book *Ethics*. In the 16th century, [[Giordano Bruno]] held pantheistic views and was burned at the stake by the [[Inquisition]]. In the East, Advaita Vedanta, a school of [[Hindu philosophy]], is thought similar to pantheism, and the early [[Taoism]] of Laozi and Zhuangzi is sometimes considered pantheistic. Cheondoism, which arose in the [[Joseon]] Dynasty of Korea, is also considered pantheistic. Pantheism is not the same as [[Panentheism|panentheism]], which holds that divinity is greater than the universe.

Ancient temple in [[Rome]], Italy, later a Roman Catholic church. Originally built under Roman emperor [[Augustus]] (27 BC–AD 14) and reconstructed under [[Hadrian]] (117–138), it was probably dedicated c. AD 126. Hadrian re-inscribed the new temple with Agrippa's original date, so its construction date is uncertain. Since AD 609 it has served as a basilica of Saint Mary and the Holy Martyrs, and it is one of the best-preserved ancient Roman buildings because it has been in continuous use. Its round rotunda, behind a [[Granite|granite]] Corinthian portico, is covered by a coffered [[Concrete|concrete]] [[Dome|dome]] with an oculus open to the sky. The height to the oculus equals the interior diameter, 43 m (142 ft). The dome remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, and the design became a model for later architects after classical styles were revived.

Genus of big cats in the family [[Felidae]], containing the largest living members of the cat family. The five living species are the [[Jaguar]], [[Leopard]], [[Lion]], [[Snow leopard]] and [[Tiger]]. Only the snow leopard cannot roar, because its vocal folds, 9 mm (0.35 in) long, are shorter than those of other species. Panthera diverged from other cats about 11.3 million years ago. The earliest known definitive species, *Panthera principialis*, is from [[Tanzania]].

German medium tank used extensively in [[World War II]]. Developed in the late 1930s, it was designed for infantry support and armed with a short-barreled 75 mm [[Howitzer|howitzer]]. As the Germans faced the Soviet [[T-34]], it was upgraded with thicker armor and more powerful guns. It was the most numerous German tank of the war, with 8,553 built, and the only German tank in continuous production throughout the war. Its chassis was also used for other vehicles, including the Sturmgeschütz IV assault gun. Panzer IVs that Syria procured after the war saw combat in the 1967 [[Six-Day War]].

Italian football executive and former defender. He spent all 25 seasons of his playing career with [[AC Milan]] in [[Serie A]], making a club record 902 appearances and winning 26 trophies, including five [[UEFA Champions League]] titles. Captain of Milan and Italy for many years, he was nicknamed "Il Capitano". He played 126 times for Italy and reached the final of the 1994 [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] and of Euro 2000. Maldini retired in 2009 and later worked as sporting director at Milan from 2018 to 2023.

Cervical screening method that detects precancerous and cancerous changes in the [[Cervix|cervix]]. Also called a Pap smear, it was independently invented in the 1920s by the Greek physician Georgios Papanikolaou. A simplified version was introduced by the Canadian obstetrician Anna Marion Hilliard in 1957. Cells are collected from the transformation zone of the cervix with a spatula or cytobrush and examined under a [[Microscope|microscope]] for abnormalities. The test aims to detect changes caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), and it remains an effective, widely used method for early detection of precancer and cervical [[Cancer|cancer]]. Screening usually begins in adulthood and is typically recommended every three to five years if results are normal. Abnormal results may lead to repeat testing in six to twelve months or to colposcopy, which magnifies the view of the cervix, vagina and vulva.

Territories on the Italian Peninsula under the direct sovereign rule of the pope, from 756 to 1870. The state was established in the 8th century, when Pepin the Short, king of the [[Franks]], gave Pope Stephen II lands formerly held by the [[Lombards]]. Its territory expanded greatly during the [[Early modern period|early modern period]], and at its zenith it covered most of the modern regions of Lazio, including Rome, Marche, Umbria, Romagna and parts of Emilia. By 1860 much of the territory had been conquered by the Kingdom of Sardinia and incorporated into the [[Kingdom of Italy]] in 1861. Lazio, including Rome, was annexed in 1870. In 1929 [[Benito Mussolini]] negotiated the Lateran Treaty, which acknowledged the sovereignty of the [[Holy See]] over [[Vatican City]], a new city-state within Rome.

Species of flowering plant in the poppy family, also called the opium poppy or breadseed poppy. It is the source of both [[Opium|opium]] and poppy seeds, and it is also grown as an ornamental plant. Its native range is the western Mediterranean, but widespread introduction and cultivation since ancient times have obscured it. [[Carl Linnaeus]] gave it its accepted name in 1753. Grown as an agricultural crop, it is used to produce poppy seeds, opium for the pharmaceutical industry, and other [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]], mainly thebaine and oripavine. All parts of the plant exude white latex when wounded.

Tropical fruit plant, *Carica papaya*, in the family Caricaceae. It was first domesticated in [[Mesoamerica]], in present-day southern Mexico and Central America, and is now grown in tropical regions worldwide. In 2024 India was the leading producer, accounting for 36% of the world total. The plant usually has a single stem 5 to 10 m (16 to 33 ft) tall, topped by large leaves. Its fruit is a large berry that ripens to an amber to orange skin. Papaya skin, pulp, and seeds contain [[Carotenoid|carotenoids]] and polyphenols. The green fruit contains papain, a cysteine protease [[Enzyme|enzyme]] used to tenderize meat. Spaniards introduced the plant to the Old World in the 16th century.

Negotiable promissory note payable to the bearer on demand, and a form of currency. The main types are government notes, issued directly by political authorities, and banknotes, issued by [[Bank|banks]] including central banks. Paper money is often, but not always, legal tender. Counterfeiting is an inherent challenge, and fighting it has been a principal driver of security printing methods in recent centuries. The first documented paper money appeared in [[China]] in the 7th century, during the [[Tang dynasty]], as merchants' deposit receipts called "flying money" that spared them the bulk of coinage. The [[Song dynasty]] issued the first generally circulating notes, called *jiaozi*, by the 11th century. In 1661 Stockholms Banco in [[Sweden]] made the first European attempt at issuing banknotes. The [[French Revolution]] brought mass issuance of government notes that collapsed in value, and [[Napoleon]] then established the Bank of France to issue banknotes in the early 1800s.

Spice made from dried and ground red peppers, *Capsicum annuum*. Sweet paprika is mainly the fruit with most seeds removed, while hotter varieties retain some seeds and stalks. Peppers reached Western Europe via Spain and Portugal in the 16th century, and [[Christopher Columbus]] probably came across them on his first voyage in 1492. Paprika was taken up in the [[Ottoman Empire]], which ruled central Hungary for much of the 16th and 17th centuries. Central European paprika was hot until the 1920s, when a Szeged breeder found a plant with sweet fruit. Paprika is a major ingredient in the cuisines of Hungary, Serbia, Spain and Portugal.

Island country in [[Melanesia]], in Oceania, comprising the eastern half of [[New Guinea]] and offshore islands. Its capital is [[Port Moresby]]. Germany and Britain divided the eastern half of New Guinea in 1884. [[Australia]] took over the British portion in 1902 and occupied the German portion during World War I. The two territories were united in 1949, and Papua New Guinea became independent in 1975 as a [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth realm]]. Its politics follow a Westminster system, with a prime minister and the monarch represented by a governor-general. With 840 known spoken languages, it is the most linguistically diverse country in the world. Only 14% of the population lived in urban centers in 2023, and nearly 40% are subsistence farmers. Official estimates put the population at about 11.8 million, while satellite data suggest closer to 17 million. In March 2025 its constitution was amended to adopt Christianity as the official state religion.

Writing material made from the pith of the wetland sedge *Cyperus papyrus*. It was first manufactured in [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]] in the 3rd millennium BCE, and Egyptians also used the reeds for boats, mats, rope, sandals, and baskets. Papyrus rolls excavated in 2012 and 2013 date from c. 2560–2550 BCE and describe the final years of building the [[Great Pyramid of Giza]]. Papyrus was rolled into [[Scroll|scrolls]], and later sheets were cut to form [[Codex|codices]]. [[Parchment]], made from animal skins, gradually replaced papyrus in West Asia and Europe because it was more durable in moist climates and could be written on both sides. Papyrus use in Egypt continued until less expensive [[Paper|paper]], introduced by the Islamic world, replaced it.

Mirror-symmetrical, approximately U-shaped plane curve and a [[Conic section|conic section]]. It is the set of points equidistant from a fixed point, the focus, and a fixed line, the directrix. A parabola is also the graph of a quadratic function, y = ax² + bx + c. Light traveling parallel to its axis of symmetry is reflected to the focus, a property used in parabolic antennas, microphones, telescopes, and headlight reflectors. [[Apollonius of Perga]] gave the curve its name, and [[Archimedes]] calculated the area of a parabolic segment in the 3rd century BC. When [[Isaac Newton]] built the first reflecting telescope in 1668, he used a spherical mirror because a parabolic one was difficult to make.

Swiss physician, alchemist, and philosopher of the German [[Renaissance]]. He was a pioneer of the medical revolution of the Renaissance, emphasizing observation alongside received wisdom, and is credited as the father of [[Toxicology|toxicology]]. He introduced mineral and chemical remedies, such as mercury for treating [[Syphilis]], and rejected the humoral theories of [[Galen]] and [[Avicenna]]. He wrote that "solely the dose determines that a thing is not a poison." In [[Alchemy|alchemy]], he proposed that all matter consists of three principles: sulfur, mercury, and salt. Briefly a professor at [[Basel]] in 1527–1528, he was ousted after conflicts with established physicians. His writings often blended medicine, alchemy, and theology.

[[Analgesic]] and antipyretic drug used to treat fever and mild to moderate pain. Also called acetaminophen, it is sold over the counter under brand names such as Tylenol and Panadol. It is the most commonly used medication for pain and fever in the United States and Europe, and it is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines. It is the first-line treatment for pain and fever in [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. It is often used by patients who cannot tolerate [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Evidence that it reduces fever is limited, and it has been described as over-prescribed for that purpose. Overdose can cause liver failure, and paracetamol poisoning is the foremost cause of acute [[Liver|liver]] failure in many countries.

Device that slows an object's descent through an [[Atmosphere|atmosphere]] by creating [[Drag (physics)|drag]] or [[Lift (force)|aerodynamic lift]]. It is mainly used to support people leaving aircraft, but it also slows cargo, aids space capsule recovery, and lands spacecraft on other planets. Modern parachutes are typically made of [[Nylon|nylon]]. In AD 852 Armen Firman is recorded as jumping in Córdoba, Spain, with a large cloak to slow his fall. [[Leonardo da Vinci]] sketched designs resembling modern parachutes, but the first successful jumps came in the 18th century. The [[France|Frenchman]] Louis-Sébastien Lenormand made the first public jump in 1783 and coined the term in 1785. After [[World War II]], parachuting became a popular sport, and nylon replaced [[Silk|silk]].

Distinct set of concepts or thought patterns, including theories, research methods, postulates, and standards for legitimate contributions to a field. The word comes from [[Ancient Greek]] *parádeigma*, meaning "pattern" or "example." In linguistics, [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] used the term for a class of elements with similarities. The historian of science Thomas Kuhn gave the word its contemporary meaning in *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* (1962). For Kuhn, a paradigm is a set of accepted achievements that provide model problems and solutions to a community of practitioners. Normal science proceeds within a paradigm until anomalies accumulate and a paradigm shift occurs. The term is closely related to the discussion of theory-ladenness in the [[Philosophy of science|philosophy of science]]. In grammar, a paradigm is a systematic table of the inflected forms of a word.

Place of everlasting happiness, delight, and bliss in religion and folklore. Paradisiacal notions often feature pastoral imagery and contrast with the miseries of human civilization. Paradise is often described as a higher place, in contrast to this world or to underworlds such as hell. The word derives from Greek *parádeisos*, used in the [[Septuagint]] to mean "garden" or "orchard." The Latin *paradisus* in the [[Vulgate]] translation of Genesis 2:8 led to its use for the [[Garden of Eden]]. In eschatological contexts, paradise is an abode of the virtuous dead. In Judaism, Christianity, and [[Islam]], heaven is a paradisiacal belief. In [[Hinduism]] and [[Buddhism]], paradise and heaven are synonymous, with higher levels for those who attain special virtue and meditation. The concept is a theme in art and literature, notably John Milton's *Paradise Lost*.
